findings.message: the solver's own solution, written from the prompt alone, does not pass every test in the sandbox
findings.resolution: Fixed: the empty-list test was removed because the valid formula n * (n - 1) / 2 returns -0 there and failed on strict comparison, and a 5-item test was added.

findings.message: arrays.lesson-3: The worked example declares `const top = pile.pop();` at the top level. In a browser, `top` is a non-configurable property of the global window, so a top-level `const top` (or let) throws a SyntaxError (identifier already declared). A learner who copies the card into a browser console or script gets an error instead of `3 [1, 2]`. It only works in the pipeline runner or inside a function or module. Rename the variable (for example `last`).
findings.resolution: Fixed: the worked example now names the popped value last instead of top, which clashes with the browser global.

findings.message: The snippet never reads a let or const before its declaration line has run, so the item can be solved with no knowledge of the temporal dead zone. It is plain sequential tracing, and the NaN distractor (price treated as undefined) is implausible because line 3 visibly runs before line 4. The item does not exercise the concept of its lesson.
findings.resolution: Fixed: rewrote the trace so a block reads its own let size before line 6 declares it, which throws a ReferenceError, with an outer size of 2 as the tempting wrong read.

findings.message: Two lines can fairly be called the bug. Line 2 (const old = deal;) is where the stale copy is made, and line 3 is where it is used. The prompt does not say which one to tap, and all three replacement options only make sense for line 3. A careful learner who taps line 2 as the root cause has no matching fix, and only hint 1 (Look at which variable line 3 subtracts) settles it.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the prompt now says to tap the line that reads the stale value, which is line 3 and matches all three replacement options (version 2).

findings.message: Hint 3 ('Define the object and the function first, then bind, then call') spells out the whole line order of the solution, so nothing is left to work out; it states the answer instead of coming near it.
findings.resolution: Fixed: hint 3 now tells the learner to work backwards from the console.log line and ask which names each line needs, instead of spelling out the order.

findings.message: Hint 3 says 'call weigh with it', but the prompt never names a function weigh; the learner chooses the name. The hint (and the explanation) refer to an identifier the learner has not seen and may not have used.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the prompt now names the function weigh that the learner must define, so hint 3 and the explanation refer to a known identifier.

findings.message: Feedback of the option 'twin is copied to every instance' says 'static keeps the method on the class itself. The output shows p has no twin.' That restates the correct option and the observed result, so the wrong-option feedback reveals the right answer instead of only addressing the mistaken belief.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the wrong option's feedback no longer restates the correct answer or the output, and points only to comparing lines 7 and 9.

findings.message: The prompt says Return 'name: low' in quotes. A careful learner can read that as the literal string name: low, but the tests expect the item's name property (ink: low, pens: ok). The quoted text should show that name stands for item.name, for example by saying 'the item name, a colon and a space, then low'.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the prompt now says to return the item's name, a colon, a space and low (or ok), so name clearly stands for the item's name.

findings.message: Feedback of the third option says 'Every function has a prototype object from the start'. This is false for arrow functions and method shorthand, which have no prototype property. It should say that a constructor function has one from the start. Low severity: the item is about constructor functions.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the third option feedback now says a constructor function has a prototype object from the start, which is true for the code shown (version 3).

findings.message: Hint 3 ('Call next() once without printing, then print the value of the second call') states the exact order of the last two lines, so it gives the solution instead of narrowing the choice.
findings.resolution: Fixed: hint 3 no longer states the order of the last two lines; it asks how many next() calls are needed to reach 9 (version 2).

findings.message: Hint 3 tells the learner to 'keep an object of names seen so far' and add 1 for a new name, which steers toward a plain object used as a set with a truthy or 'in' check. A hidden test ({names: ['toString']} expecting 1) rejects exactly that approach, because 'toString' is inherited. Neither the prompt nor hints 1 to 3 warn about inherited names (only the explanation does, after the fact), so a learner who follows the hints correctly fails a test about an unrelated quirk.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the prompt says a name can be any text and hint 3 warns that a name counts as seen only if recorded itself, not inherited.

findings.message: Hint 3 says 'Return only the weight.' That is the content of the correct replacement line (return this.kg;) and it also rules out both wrong options, so the learner no longer has to reason about what valueOf must return. The README says a hint never states the answer.
findings.resolution: Fixed: hint 3 no longer says to return only the weight; it asks which kind of primitive makes + add the crates instead of joining them (version 3).

findings.message: The reference points to the MDN page for the break statement, but this item has no break and is about repeating work inside a loop (and reduce). A learner who follows the link to read more lands on an unrelated topic.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the reference now points to the MDN page for Array.prototype.reduce, which the item's code uses.

findings.message: Hint 3 spells out the correct replacement in order ('a new empty object, then the old values, then the new size'). That is exactly Object.assign({}, s, { size }) and also rules out the third option, whose only difference is the argument order, so the learner no longer has to reason about which source wins.
findings.resolution: Fixed: hint 3 now asks the learner to compare the first argument and the source order in the options instead of listing the replacement.

findings.message: This is the first TRACE of the course and it needs a declared variable that is reassigned (let tray = 12; tray = tray / 4). let and reassignment are taught in the next unit (Variables: let-declaration, reassignment), and this unit has no earlier unit and declares no prerequisite for them. The same dependency recurs in string-values.trace-01, boolean-values.predict-01 and trace-01, and typeof-operator.trace-01; it is filed here as the first item it concerns. The lesson card for lesson 1 must teach declaring and reassigning a variable, or the TRACE slots must avoid reassignment.
findings.resolution: Not a defect: let and reassignment are taught in this very unit (constructs.json maps let-const to values-and-types, and the lesson 1 card says a let line stores a value a later line can replace).

findings.message: Needs method-call syntax on a value ("  tea  ".trim()) and knowledge of what trim does. Neither is taught earlier (this is the first unit), and the concept of the lesson is joining text, not string methods. Method calls are first introduced with push/pop in the Arrays unit.
findings.resolution: Fixed: replaced the untaught trim call with toUpperCase, which the lesson 2 card teaches, in a three-line snippet that shows the method returns new text (version 2, misconceptions updated).

findings.message: Both blanks are method names called on a string ("bread".___()). Method-call syntax and the case methods toUpperCase/toLowerCase are neither taught earlier nor part of the lesson concept (strings and joining text), so the item tests recalling API names the learner has not met.
findings.resolution: Fixed: reduced the item to one blank filled by toUpperCase (taught on the card), dropped toLowerCase and trim, and made every other chip fail with an error (version 2).

findings.message: typeof undefined needs the value undefined, which is taught in the next unit (Variables, undefined-and-null, whose own prerequisite is this typeof lesson). The learner has not met undefined here, and the concept list of this unit does not include it.
findings.resolution: Fixed: replaced typeof undefined with typeof typeof 5 (string), which needs only taught ideas, and updated the lesson 4 card to stop mentioning undefined (version 3).

findings.message: typeof null returning object is the core of the later undefined-and-null lesson in the Variables unit, which repeats it in predict-02, fill-01 and trace-01. Here the learner has not been taught null, and the quirk cannot be derived, so the item tests a later unit's concept.
findings.resolution: Fixed: replaced typeof null with typeof 3.5 (number) so the item tests a typeof-lesson idea, and removed the now-unused null-and-undefined-confused misconception (version 4).

findings.message: One of the four lines is typeof null, whose result (object) can only be known from the null quirk taught in the later undefined-and-null lesson; the ordering cannot be solved without it.
findings.resolution: Fixed: removed the typeof null line and reordered the three remaining lines (boolean, string, number), so no later-unit quirk is needed (version 2).

findings.message: The snippet never reads a variable before its declaration; it is a plain let/const sequence (reassign, then multiply). It does not exercise the temporal dead zone, the lesson's concept; its only link is a distractor for the misconception that a let is undefined early.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the snippet now reads a let binding inside its dead zone in one scope with no function, so it tests the temporal dead zone.

findings.message: Marked 3, but it is a four-line straight-line trace with one reassignment and one multiplication, which is beginner-level (1) for this material, not intermediate 3.
findings.resolution: Fixed: the new item needs the shadowing and dead-zone reasoning and ends on a thrown error, so difficulty 3 now fits the Intermediate band.

findings.message: The snippet relies on btn.append('!') and btn.append('?') to add text to an element. Lesson 2 teaches only textContent, classList and createElement/appendChild, and appendChild cannot take a string, so append with text is a new DOM method that is neither declared nor taught earlier. Using textContent += would keep the item on taught ground.
findings.resolution: Fixed: replaced btn.append with textContent += on taught ground, using a short handler name and button variable to respect the 36-character limit; the expected output is now Book12 (version 2).

findings.message: The crux of this ordering is that removing an item shifts the later ones down, so click index 2 before index 1. That tests live children indexing and element.remove(), not bubbling or delegation. The single listener on the list is only scenery, and remove() has not been taught.
findings.resolution: Fixed: rewrote the ordering around one listener on the list that records e.target.id of clicked items, so bubbling and delegation are the crux; remove() and index shifting are gone (version 2).

findings.message: The Advanced recipe says FILL_BLANK or PARSONS alternate between lessons. This unit uses FILL_BLANK in lessons 1 and 2, then PARSONS in lessons 3 and 4 (fill, fill, parsons, parsons), so the alternation breaks at lesson 2. The sibling unit promises-in-depth alternates fill, parsons, fill, parsons.
